hooks.evidence: She wanted to stand up and shout. She wanted to ask why the sluice gate had been opened with a key, not by the usual mechanism.
hooks.note: Nell begins investigating the murder theory by noticing inconsistencies in the official accident verdict at the inquest, starting her pursuit against the town's acceptance of the accident ruling.

hooks.evidence: He found out, you see," Vane said, his voice dropping to a confidential murmur. "About the Drainage Board money. He was a fool, trusting me with it. He went to the bank, asked for an audit. I saw the letter he'd written. It was all over for me.
hooks.note: Ambrose Vane confesses to using the third key to open the sluice gate and push Owen Tarrant into the race.
The silver bosun's whistle from H.M.S. Cormorant 1916 is never mentioned again after chapter 2, and its significance is never revealed in the subsequent chapters.

The conflict with Bea over her marriage to Leonard Fawley is not resolved in any of the chapters provided. Bea leaves for Canada in chapter 4, and there is no further mention of her or the resolution of their conflict in chapters 3-13.

answer dropped: the quote is not in chapter 12 (said: Ambrose lied about his whereabouts because he was at the sluice gate committing the murder to cover up his embezzlement from the Drainage Board fund.)

hooks.evidence: That night, I waited.
hooks.note: Vane directly admits he was at the sluice gate the night of the murder, contradicting his alibi that he was at home in town.
The chapters show Nell confronting Ambrose with ledger evidence, not mud evidence as specified in the hook.
The chapters confirm Ambrose was skimming funds, but this information comes from his confession and Dorrit's investigation, not from Nell's own thorough investigation of his financial dealings.

hooks.evidence: I, Owen Tarrant, being of sound mind and body, do hereby revoke all previous bequests to my junior partner, Ambrose Vane. Upon my death, the partnership between myself and Ambrose Vane is hereby dissolved, and he shall receive no further share in the mill or its profits. Furthermore, all books and documents pertaining to the Fen Drainage Board fund, currently held in trust by the mill, are to be surrendered directly to the manager of the Fen & County Bank for immediate audit.
hooks.note: The will reveals Tarrant discovered Vane was stealing from the Drainage Board funds and changed his will to revoke Vane's bequests and expose the embezzlement, providing a clear motive for murder.

hooks.evidence: Nell reached out and took the ledger from the safe. It was heavy, solid proof of Vane's guilt.
hooks.note: Nell finds the missing ledger in the safe at the mill office, which contains evidence of Vane's financial crimes.

hooks.evidence: I hid it there after," Vane said with a shrug. "And the last ledger... I burned it. It had the incriminating figures.
hooks.note: Vane confesses to using the mill office lantern during the murder and hiding it in the reeds, confirming he had access to it.

hooks.evidence: I've baited the trap," she said quietly. "I told Vane the missing ledger has turned up and that Hollis is collecting it from the mill office safe tomorrow morning.
hooks.note: Nell continues pursuing the investigation by setting a trap for Vane despite the danger, obtaining concrete evidence (the ledger) that leads to his arrest.

hooks.evidence: I pushed him in.
hooks.note: Ambrose Vane confesses to being at the mill office and pushing Owen Tarrant into the sluice race, confirming he was the one with the lantern.

hooks.evidence: He was right there, looking over the edge. I just... gave him a push. He didn't even scream.
hooks.note: Vane confesses he took the key the night of the murder and lied about it being missing for months to cover up his crime.

hooks.evidence: There's no entry for three hundred pounds from Tarrant's Mill. There's an entry for two hundred.
hooks.note: Nell and Kit discover Vane has been skimming money from the Drainage Board fund by underreporting payments from the mill, keeping the difference for himself.

hooks.evidence: I hid it there after,
hooks.note: Ambrose Vane confesses he hid the lantern in the reeds after committing the murder to conceal his involvement.

hooks.evidence: The missing hundred pounds was a ghost, a sum that had been written out of the mill's books as if it had never existed.
hooks.note: Nell discovers the financial discrepancies in the drainage board records, connecting the missing ledger to Vane's embezzlement.

hooks.note: Nell confronts Ambrose at the mill office with her evidence, leading to his confession of murder.
Ambrose Vane is caught and arrested once Nell obtains the truth, rather than becoming more dangerous as she gets closer to it.

None of the chapters show Nell explicitly understanding or investigating the connection between the will codicil and the missing financial records. The information is provided through Kit, but not through Nell's own investigation or understanding.
